props.title: The Child

sections.content: The Child (L'Enfant) (2005) marks a devastating pinnacle in the Dardenne brothers' exploration of moral crisis in working-class Belgium. The film follows Bruno, a young petty criminal who sells his newborn son on the black market, then must desperately try to undo his horrific choice. Like their earlier masterpiece Rosetta (1999), the Dardennes employ their signature documentary-like style - handheld cameras, natural lighting, and zero non-diegetic music. This raw aesthetic amplifies the gut-punch of Bruno's choices. The film shares DNA with other European social realist classics like Bicycle Thieves (1948), examining how poverty corrupts fundamental human bonds.

sections.content: The Dardennes' influence resonates through contemporary social realist cinema. Fish Tank (2009) and The Florida Project (2017) echo their intimate portrayal of marginalized lives, while Shoplifters (2018) similarly interrogates how economic desperation warps family bonds. The handheld urgency of their style has become a grammar for depicting working-class struggle, seen in everything from American Honey (2016) to Never Rarely Sometimes Always (2020). SUBHEAD: The New Wave of Social Realism

While the Dardennes helped codify modern social realist cinema, filmmakers like Ken Loach and Mike Leigh laid crucial groundwork. Kes (1969) and Naked (1993) established the brutal honesty and class consciousness that define the genre. Contemporary directors like Andrea Arnold and Sean Baker carry this torch, though with distinctive stylistic flourishes - American Honey (2016) infuses its realism with dreamy Americana, while Tangerine (2015) brings saturated color and frenetic energy to its street-level story.
